$comment: Written by Claude in session against data/surveys/haresfield-beacon.json. Proper nouns limited to facts.named_features plus data/gazetteer.txt; every number agrees with the surveyed geometry. No API call — see scripts/author.py.

editorial.summary: A short circuit over the escarpment edge at Haresfield Beacon, north-west of Stroud.
editorial.character: Five kilometres and 260 m of climbing is a steep ratio, and the walk feels it: this is a short outing with a real hill in it rather than a stroll that happens to rise. The pull onto the edge touches one in six, which is brief enough not to matter and steep enough to notice, and the top then runs level along the break of slope with the ground falling away west. Nothing on the route is sealed — not a metre of it — which for a circuit this close to a main valley is unusual and is most of why it is worth the drive.
editorial.grain: The bench the path follows is the Inferior Oolite standing on Lias clay, which is why the top is dry and firm and the slope below it slips.
editorial.conditions: The edge faces west, so the last hour of light is the reason to be up there and the middle of a summer day is not. Half the route has no surface tag at all and the rest is soft going, so after a wet week the climb will be greasy and the descent more so. Winter is the honest recommendation, when the beeches are bare and the vale is legible from the top.
editorial.practical: Three car parks sit within about 600 to 800 m of where the circuit begins, none of them named in the survey and none with a recorded fee, so the charge is unknown rather than absent. No toilets and no refreshment were found within reach of the route, which also means there is no vegan provision to report either way — this is a walk to bring a flask to.
editorial.caveats: About seven tenths of the length carries a public footpath designation; the remainder is mapped but undesignated, so access there rests on the open-access status of the land rather than on anything recorded against the path. A ford is flagged on or beside the route, with nothing known about its depth or whether a footbridge stands alongside — after rain that is the thing most likely to turn this into an out-and-back. Field furniture is invisible to a survey of this kind: stiles and gates that have rotted or been replaced will not appear until they are underfoot.

confidence.basis: Seven tenths of the length is designated public footpath and the rest is open-access land, so access is better recorded than most. Against that: half the route has no surface tag, a ford is flagged with no depth or footbridge information, and the circuit is machine-assembled from OSM ways and has not been walked.
